analysis: Brokskat bizi nia twenty-nine contains twenty plus nine with a possible connective. It is a renewed compound, not a single inherited ūnatriṁśat or navaviṁśati form. Printed stress spacing must be checked before assigning component accent.
Brokskat hen up(hill) is not a visible adhyadhi reflex. A local directional particle or contact spatial term is possible; its short unmarked form has no secure old accent comparison.

Ushojo hunati bajema upward is a spatial phrase plus a go/motion present form, not a simple adverb. The hunati component may share huna-type upper spatial morphology, but no whole-expression Sanskrit ancestor is assigned; stress belongs to the actual phrase.

Brokskat tshus urine resembles Tibetan/Purik chu water with additional morphology, but donor meaning and final s require verification. It does not directly match mūtra or mēha; keep it an unresolved likely contact/material term.

Ushojo šinoṭo moṣ urine pairs with baṛo moṣ feces, literally a small/big excretion contrast. Moṣ may belong to the mēha urine family, but the modifier is independently derived and carries the written stress. Do not count the whole phrase as an unextended mēha reflex.

Brokskat ben is merged under village and we from separate table items. The we member may belong to vayam/bɨɨ, while village requires an independent settlement term; source vowel reading and lexical splitting are mandatory before family or accent counts.

Ushojo piada bo walk contains the regional Persian-derived piyāda on foot plus go bo. This is a phrasal construction with a borrowed modifier, not an inherited tillati walking verb; its medial stress cannot be projected onto an Old Indo-Aryan walk root.

Brokskat tonze and Ushojo hila wasp do not clearly match bhramara, varola or tantra-vābha. Distinct local insect names or contact terms are plausible. Their final stresses remain documented, but neither is assigned to a weaving root merely because another language calls wasps/spiders that.

Ushojo taṛnao waterchute at a mill looks compound-like and could include a channel/boat-shaped conduit term. It is not a yantra reflex simply because it is part of a mill. The medial/final stress and unequal ao sequence need independent constituent analysis.

Ushojo aso is given for both inclusive and exclusive we, so no clusivity contrast is demonstrated. The form is a strong candidate for an asmad/as- first-person oblique-derived paradigm rather than vayam, but the precise old case and analogy must be checked; initial stress is explicit.

Ushojo pon web/nest may designate woven shelter, but māna nest lacks the expected initial p and path panthā would require a semantic bridge. Preserve the polysemy and do not select either by one matching gloss.

Ushojo apta week is the regional hafta loan with h loss and cluster adaptation. Final stress is contact-word adaptation, not a direct saptá seven reflex despite the word's ultimate Iranian numeral history.

SchmidtKaul2008p248 explicitly identifies nub west, cayma willow and jokyr year as Purik loans. Stored canma and lokyr require printed reading. They are replacements, not inherited vēta/kāla accent outcomes.

Ushojo ji and Brokskat yee what may belong to a shared palatal interrogative/relative development, but kím would require an independently demonstrated initial change and the forms could be nominal thing expressions. Neither is assigned to kīdṛśa by vague resemblance; no accent is marked.

Ushojo koon te where is a k-interrogative plus spatial/postpositional te expression. The noun/pronoun and case/postposition need separate etymologies; no whole-word kúha derivation or accent outcome is imposed.

Ushojo kaamik which has a long initial-stressed k-interrogative base plus mik/ik morphology. It may contain an indefinite/comparative suffix, but kím is not the immediate whole form; retain a grammatical analysis pending the interrogative paradigm.
Ushojo ṛox whole is distinct from pūra, sāra and sarva. A complete/intact or healthy adjective could underlie the meaning, but no secure root or accent is known; it remains a lexical replacement.

Ushojo ṛiṇḍi widow strongly suggests the regional raṇḍā/raṇḍī widow family, rather than kuṇḍa or muṭṭa. The family is absent from the current automatic candidates; verify full Turner and borrowing status before accepting a new research family. Initial stress and feminine i are explicit.

Brokskat yys and Ushojo oš wind may reflect a strongly contracted vāyu/vāta-related or regional wind term, but final s/š needs independent explanation. No connection to chaṭṭa sudden movement follows from the gloss; preserve them as unresolved wind vocabulary.

Brokskat chi gaa woman may contain a female/strī-derived base plus gaa, or the spacing may be a reading artifact. Its relation to straika/cei is plausible but must be established from the printed form and Brokskat morphology, not the English gloss.

Ushojo japai woman differs from its cai wife and may contain an affinal/kinship compound or a local female term. A jāmātṛ connection would need semantic and morphological evidence; the unmarked ai sequence supplies no secure accent value.

Ushojo gonje wrinkle may be a fold/crease noun rather than a rub verb. A contraction or regional guñj/goñj formation is possible, but āmārayati is rejected as accidental meaning overlap; initial stress is documented.

Ushojo likhona write (present) clearly contains the likh writing root plus on/a morphology. It can be compared with likhati, but a local inherited versus regional borrowed verb and its actual paradigm must be established before an old accent comparison. Medial stress is on the extended stem.

Brokskat saar year plausibly adapts Iranian sāl with l-to-r, contrasting with the explicitly Purik jokyr alternative. Verify the source discussion/donor; it should not be assigned to kāla or varṣa as an inherited reflex.

Ushojo canoro yellow does not straightforwardly match haridra or pītala. A pale/bright or material-derived adjective with or/o morphology is plausible; medial stress is observed, but the independent root remains unidentified.
Ushojo ha yes is an affirmative/discourse particle with no securely selected old lexical ancestor. Such a short particle may be prosodically dependent or expressive; no marked accent is present.

Ushojo bealuku yesterday resembles the byala/vikāla evening-time set with additional uku morphology. The suffix and unequal ea sequence must be explained before accepting vikāla versus vikālāhāra; late stress is a formation-level observation, not direct old root inheritance.

Ushojo so/tso formal you and so buṭe plural you belong to a politeness/plural paradigm, perhaps linked to a tus/yuṣmad development or third-person demonstrative politeness. The buṭe all modifier makes the second a phrase. Do not choose the old second-person input without paradigm evidence.
